title: Fix Scheduler.toExecutorService() NullPointerException from null worker store
bug:
The no-arg `Scheduler.toExecutorService()` passes `null` for the `SchedulerToExecutorService` worker store, so every method (`execute`/`submit`/`shutdown`/`isShutdown`/…) throws `NullPointerException` on first use via `workerStore.get()`:

```java
Schedulers.single().toExecutorService().execute(() -> {}); // NullPointerException
```

The `toExecutorService(boolean)` overload one method below already does it correctly, passing `new AtomicReference<>()`. This change makes the no-arg version consistent: with no worker present, the methods fall back to `scheduler.scheduleDirect(...)` as intended.

Adds a regression test (`SchedulerTest.toExecutorServiceWithoutWorkerExecutes`) that fails before the change (NPE) and passes after.

title: Fix IllegalStateException in SchedulerToExecutorService.invokeAny
bug:
## Problem

`SchedulerToExecutorService.invokeAny()` checks each future with:

```java
if (f.isDone() && !f.isCancelled() && f.exceptionNow() == null) {
```

But `Future.exceptionNow()` is specified to throw `IllegalStateException` when the task **completed normally** (there is no exception to return). So as soon as a task finishes successfully, this guard calls `exceptionNow()` on a successfully-completed future and throws `IllegalStateException` instead of returning the result. Both `invokeAny` overloads contain the same probe.

## Fix

Use the intended state query, which never throws:

```java
if (f.state() == Future.State.SUCCESS) {
```

## Test

Adds `SchedulerToExecutorServiceTest` covering the success paths. The new `invokeAnyShouldReturnResultOfCompletedTask` and `invokeAnyWithSingleTask` tests fail on `master` with `IllegalStateException` and pass with this fix.

Note: the timed `invokeAny(tasks, timeout, unit)` overload has a separate pre-existing issue in its time accounting (the `FIXME`-marked spin loop) that this PR intentionally does not touch; it only addresses the `exceptionNow()` misuse.

suspicion.observation: SchedulerToExecutorService.invokeAny() calls f.exceptionNow() on a CompletableFuture. In Java, CompletableFuture.exceptionNow() is designed for internal JDK use and throws IllegalStateException when the future was completed normally (not exceptionally). Since all submitted tasks complete normally, this always throws IllegalStateException in the isDone() check path.
suspicion.suspected_bug: invokeAny() throws IllegalStateException instead of returning results because CompletableFuture.exceptionNow() is misused - it throws when the future completed normally rather than exceptionally.

title: Treat prefix literally in UrlTemplate.match(url, prefix)
bug:
## Problem

`UrlTemplate.match(url, prefix)` strips the prefix with:

```java
matchAgainst = matchAgainst.replaceFirst(prefix, "");
```

`String.replaceFirst` treats its first argument as a **regular expression**, so a prefix containing regex metacharacters is mis-handled. For example a prefix with an unmatched `(` throws `PatternSyntaxException`; other metacharacters can silently strip the wrong text.

## Fix

Quote the prefix with `Pattern.quote(prefix)` so it is matched literally.

## Test

Adds `shouldNotThrowWhenPrefixContainsRegexMetacharacters` to `UrlTemplateTest`: matching with a prefix containing `(` throws `PatternSyntaxException` on `trunk` and succeeds with this change.

suspicion.observation: UrlTemplate.match(String, String) uses replaceFirst(prefix, "") where replaceFirst treats the first argument as a regex pattern. If the prefix contains regex special characters (like '.', '[', '(', etc.), it will either throw an exception or produce incorrect matching behavior.
suspicion.suspected_bug: Calling match(url, prefix) where prefix contains regex meta-characters will produce wrong results or throw PatternSyntaxException because replaceFirst interprets prefix as a regex.

title: Make Either.stream() and iterator() empty for a left value
bug:
## Problem

`Either.stream()` returned `Stream.of(right())` and `Either.iterator()` returned `Collections.singleton(right()).iterator()` unconditionally, regardless of which side the `Either` holds. For a left-valued `Either`, `right()` is `null`, so:

- `stream()` yields a single `null` element (and throws `NullPointerException` in downstream operations such as `toList()` on some pipelines), and
- `iterator()` yields one `null` element instead of being empty.

A left-valued `Either` has no right value, so both should be empty — consistent with treating `Either` as a (possibly empty) collection of the right value.

## Fix

Return an empty stream / iterator when the `Either` holds a left value.

## Test

Adds `EitherTest` covering `stream()` and `iterator()` for both left and right values. The left-value cases fail on `trunk` (non-empty, containing `null`) and pass with this change.

suspicion.observation: Either.stream() calls Stream.of(right()) which will throw NullPointerException when the Either is a "left" instance (right is null). Similarly, Either.iterator() calls Collections.singleton(right()) which produces a singleton containing null, not an empty iterator, when right is null.
suspicion.suspected_bug: Calling stream() on an Either that holds only a left value will throw NullPointerException, and iterator() will return an iterator yielding a single null element instead of being empty for a left-value Either.

title: Fix FlowRuleComparator violating the Comparator contract
bug:
## Problem

`FlowRuleComparator.compare` returns `0` (equal) for rules that are not actually equal:

```java
if (o1.getLimitApp() == null) {
    return 0;                       // returns 0 even when o2.getLimitApp() is non-null
}
...
} else {
    return 0;                       // two different non-default limitApps compare as equal
}
```

So a rule whose `limitApp` is `null` compares equal to any other rule, and two rules with different non-default `limitApp` values (e.g. `originA` vs `originB`) compare equal. Returning `0` for unequal elements violates the `Comparator` contract and can cause rules to be dropped when stored in a sorted structure.

## Fix

- Return `0` only when both `limitApp`s are `null`; otherwise order a `null` consistently against a non-null value.
- Compare two different non-default `limitApp`s with `String.compareTo` instead of returning `0`.

## Test

Adds `testNullVsNonNullLimitApp` and `testDifferentNonDefaultLimitApps` to `FlowRuleComparatorTest`, each also checking antisymmetry. Both fail on `1.8` (`compare` returns `0` for unequal rules) and pass with this change.

suspicion.observation: In FlowRuleComparator.compare (lines 40-54), the logic checks `if (o1.getLimitApp() == null) { return 0; }` without checking o2. If o1.getLimitApp() is null but o2.getLimitApp() is not null, this returns 0 (equal) incorrectly. Additionally, when both are non-null but neither is DEFAULT, line 53 returns 0 even though they are different non-default apps, which violates the Comparator contract.
suspicion.suspected_bug: Comparator returns 0 (equal) when o1.getLimitApp() is null and o2.getLimitApp() is non-null, violating the Comparator contract. Also returns 0 for two different non-default apps.

title: Fix JdbcTypeUtil mapping Types.BIT/BOOLEAN to Byte instead of Boolean
bug:
## Problem

In `JdbcTypeUtil.jdbcType2javaType`, the `Types.BIT` and `Types.BOOLEAN` cases have their `return Boolean.class;` commented out:

```java
switch (jdbcType) {
    case Types.BIT:
    case Types.BOOLEAN:
        // return Boolean.class;
    case Types.TINYINT:
        return Byte.TYPE;
```

So BIT and BOOLEAN fall through to the `TINYINT` case and return `Byte.TYPE`. JDBC `BIT`/`BOOLEAN` columns are therefore mapped to `Byte` instead of `Boolean`.

## Fix

Restore `return Boolean.class;` for the BIT/BOOLEAN cases. The same bug exists in both copies of this class (`client-adapter/common` and `connector/core`), and both are fixed.

## Test

Adds `JdbcTypeUtilBitBooleanTest`: asserts `jdbcType2javaType` maps `BIT` and `BOOLEAN` to `Boolean.class` and `TINYINT` to `Byte.TYPE`. The BIT/BOOLEAN cases fail on `master` (they return `Byte.TYPE`) and pass with this change.

This means Types.BIT and Types.BOOLEAN fall through to `case Types.TINYINT:` and return `Byte.TYPE`. The same pattern exists in connector/core/src/main/java/com/alibaba/otter/canal/connector/core/util/JdbcTypeUtil.java. This is a copy-paste of the same file, so the same bug exists there.
suspicion.suspected_bug: Switch cases Types.BIT and Types.BOOLEAN fall through to Types.TINYINT because the original return statement was commented out without adding a break. This causes jdbcType2javaType(Types.BIT) and jdbcType2javaType(Types.BOOLEAN) to incorrectly return Byte.TYPE instead of Boolean.class, leading to incorrect type mapping for boolean/bit columns.

title: Fix UriUtils.parseQuery dropping query values that contain '='

suspicion.observation: In UriUtils.parseQuery(), line 62 does `String[] pair = token.split(EQUAL);` where EQUAL is "=". title: Fix trailing separator in StringUtils.join with null elements
bug:
## Problem

`StringUtils.join(Collection, String)` skips `null` elements, but it decides whether to append the separator from the element **index** (`i != collection.size() - 1`) rather than from whether another non-null element actually follows. When the collection ends with one or more `null` values, a stray trailing separator is produced:

```java
StringUtils.join(Arrays.asList("a", null), ",");          // "a,"   (expected "a")
StringUtils.join(Arrays.asList("a", null, "b", null), ","); // "a,b," (expected "a,b")
```

Leading and interior nulls combined with a trailing null are affected the same way.

## Fix

Track whether anything has been appended yet and emit the separator **before** each subsequent non-null element instead of after by index. This makes trailing, leading, and mixed null elements behave correctly while leaving the all-non-null case unchanged.

## Test

Adds `testJoinWithTrailingNulls` to `StringUtilsTest` covering trailing, leading, and mixed null cases. It fails on `develop` (`expected: <a> but was: <a,>`) and passes with this change; the full `StringUtilsTest` suite (31 tests) and `checkstyle:check` on the `common` module both pass.

suspicion.observation: In StringUtils.join(Collection, String), when iterating with index i, the separator is appended based on index position (i != collection.size() - 1), not based on whether there are more non-null elements. When the collection contains trailing null elements, a spurious trailing separator is produced. For example, join(["a", null], ",") produces "a," instead of "a".
suspicion.suspected_bug: Trailing separator bug: join(["a", null], ",") returns "a," with trailing comma, because the null-skipping logic doesn't account for the separator being added before a null element. The separator decision is based on array index, not on whether subsequent non-null elements exist.

title: Skip malformed config-plugin property names without a dot in refreshPluginProperties
bug:
## Problem

`ConfigChangeConfigs.refreshPluginProperties()` iterates the property names under the config-plugin prefix and splits each on the first dot:

```java
for (String each : properties.stringPropertyNames()) {
    int typeIndex = each.indexOf(.);
    String type = each.substring(0, typeIndex);        // typeIndex == -1 -> StringIndexOutOfBoundsException
    String subKey = each.substring(typeIndex + 1);
    ...
}
configPluginProperties = newProperties;                 // never reached if the loop threw
```

If any property name under the prefix has no dot, `indexOf(.)` returns `-1` and `substring(0, -1)` throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. The exception is caught further out, but it occurs **before** `configPluginProperties` is assigned, so every valid plugin property loaded in that pass is discarded.

## Fix

Skip property names without a dot, so a single malformed entry no longer wipes out the valid plugin properties.

## Test

Adds `testRefreshPluginPropertiesIgnoresMalformedPropertyWithoutDot` to `ConfigChangeConfigsTest`: it mocks the prefixed properties to include a valid `mockPlugin.enabled` and a malformed `nodotvalue`, and asserts the valid one is still loaded. It fails before the change (`StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` wipes the valid property) and passes after.

suspicion.observation: In ConfigChangeConfigs.refreshPluginProperties() at line 60-62, int typeIndex = each.indexOf('.') is used and then each.substring(0, typeIndex) is called. If the property name doesn't contain a dot, indexOf('.') returns -1, and substring(0, -1) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The surrounding try-catch will swallow it but the properties won't be loaded correctly.
suspicion.suspected_bug: StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when a config property name under the PREFIX doesn't contain a dot, because indexOf('.') returns -1 and is used directly as substring end index

title: Fix integer overflow in SetOperations.cosineSimilarity
bug:
## Problem

`SetOperations.cosineSimilarity` computes the product of the two cardinalities as an `int` before passing it to `Math.sqrt`:

```java
// Given that the cardinality is an int then the product as a double will not
// overflow, we can use one sqrt:
return numerator == 0 ? 0 : numerator / Math.sqrt(cardinality(first) * cardinality(second));
```

The comment states the product is meant to be computed as a `double` so it will not overflow, but without a cast the multiplication happens in `int`. For large inputs (each cardinality > 46341) the product exceeds `Integer.MAX_VALUE` and wraps to a negative value, so `Math.sqrt` returns `NaN` and both `cosineSimilarity` and `cosineDistance` become `NaN`.

For example, two identical extractors of cardinality 50000 give `50000 * 50000 = 2_500_000_000`, which overflows to a negative `int`; the similarity should be `1.0` but is `NaN`.

## Fix

Cast the first operand to `double` so the product is computed in `double`, as the comment already intended. Both the `BitMapExtractor` and `BloomFilter` overloads had the same issue and are fixed.

## Test

Adds `testCosineSimilarityLargeCardinalityNoOverflow` to `SetOperationsTest`, building extractors with cardinality 50000 and asserting `cosineSimilarity == 1.0` / `cosineDistance == 0.0`. It fails on `master` (`expected: <1.0> but was: <NaN>`) and passes with this change; the existing `SetOperationsTest` suite stays green.

suspicion.observation: In cosineSimilarity(BitMapExtractor, BitMapExtractor), the expression `cardinality(first) * cardinality(second)` performs int*int multiplication before passing to Math.sqrt. Both cardinalities return int. If both are large (e.g., each >46341), the product overflows Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647), causing incorrect results or negative values passed to sqrt. The comment on line 102 says "the product as a double will not overflow" but the multiplication is done in int, not double arithmetic.
suspicion.suspected_bug: Integer overflow in cardinality multiplication causes incorrect cosineSimilarity results for large Bloom filters

title: Avoid NegativeArraySizeException in ProxyLeakTask on short stack traces

title: Fix wrong substring range in AntPathMatcher wildcard counting
bug:
`AntPathMatcher.AntPatternComparator` counts wildcards to compare pattern specificity. When it encounters a `*`, it checks whether the preceding character makes it part of a `.*` sequence — but it uses `this.pattern.substring(pos - 1)`, which returns everything from `pos - 1` to the **end** of the pattern, not the two characters at `[pos - 1, pos]`. So for any pattern where `.*` isn't the final two characters, `.equals(".*")` is false and the `*` is miscounted as a single wildcard.

This corrupts the specificity comparison — e.g. `getPatternComparator(...).compare("/files/.*.txt", "/files/*a.txt")` returns `0` (treated as equally specific) instead of `< 0` (the `.*` pattern is more specific).

The fix restores the two-character window `substring(pos - 1, pos + 1)`, matching the original Spring `AntPathMatcher` this class is ported from. Adds a regression test.

suspicion.observation: Line 869: this.pattern.substring(pos - 1).equals(".*") - substring(pos-1) returns the entire string from pos-1 to END, not just two characters. It should be this.pattern.substring(pos - 1, pos + 1).equals(".*") to correctly check if the last two characters form ".*". This causes singleWildcards to be incorrectly counted because the comparison is almost always false when the pattern is longer than 2 chars.
suspicion.suspected_bug: Wrong substring range in pattern wildcard counting: substring(pos - 1) without end index returns rest of string instead of just two characters, causing incorrect singleWildcards count

title: Rethrow Error from @PostConstruct method instead of wrapping it in RuntimeException
bug:
`PostConstructAdapterFactory` rethrows a `RuntimeException` cause as-is, but wraps everything else (`throw new RuntimeException(e.getCause())`). An `Error` thrown by the `@PostConstruct` method — `AssertionError`, `OutOfMemoryError`, `NoClassDefFoundError`, … — is unchecked like `RuntimeException` and should propagate **unchanged**, not be wrapped in a `RuntimeException` (where a `catch (RuntimeException)` could swallow what is meant to be unrecoverable).

This adds the symmetric `else if (e.getCause() instanceof Error) throw (Error) e.getCause();`, matching how the same block already treats `RuntimeException`. The `new RuntimeException(...)` fallback stays for genuinely checked causes. Includes a regression test.

suspicion.observation: In PostConstructAdapterFactory's read method at line 62, `method.invoke(result)` can throw InvocationTargetException. The catch block at line 65 catches InvocationTargetException and re-throws the cause as RuntimeException. However, if the underlying cause is an Error (like OutOfMemoryError or StackOverflowError), it will be wrapped in a RuntimeException at line 69, which is incorrect - Errors should propagate as Errors, not be wrapped in RuntimeException.
suspicion.suspected_bug: When PostConstruct method invocation throws an Error (like OutOfMemoryError), it gets incorrectly wrapped in RuntimeException instead of being propagated as an Error, making debugging harder and violating JVM error propagation semantics.

title: Saturate count() and entryIterator() in Multisets.sum() to avoid integer overflow
bug:
`Multisets.sum(a, b)`'s `size()` already guards against overflow with `IntMath.saturatedAdd`, but `count()` and `entryIterator()` add the per-element counts with a plain `+`. When two multisets each hold close to `Integer.MAX_VALUE` of an element, the sum overflows to a **negative count** — which violates the `Multiset` contract (counts are non-negative) and makes `immutableEntry`'s `checkNonnegative` throw `IllegalArgumentException` (`count cannot be negative but was: -2147483648`).

This applies `IntMath.saturatedAdd` in `count()` and `entryIterator()`, matching what `size()` already does, so the count saturates at `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. Adds regression tests for both paths.

title: Return null from PathMatcher.buildUriFromTemplate on a template missing its closing brace
bug:
Closes #50291

## Problem

`PathMatcher.buildUriFromTemplate` replaces a `{placeholder}` using `uri.indexOf("}", lastPattern)` as the end index:

```java
if (c == '{') {
    uri.replace(uri.indexOf("{", lastPattern), uri.indexOf("}", lastPattern) + 1, value.toString());
}
```

When the template contains an opening `{` with no matching `}`, `indexOf("}", ...)` returns `-1`, so the call becomes `uri.replace(start, 0, value)` with `start > end`. That throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` (e.g. `start 5, end 0`) instead of treating the input as non-matching.

## Fix

Guard the missing-closing-brace case and return `null`, consistent with the method's other no-match results.

## Test

Adds `missingClosingBraceShouldReturnNull` to `PathMatcherTest`. It fails on `main` (`StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`) and passes with this change.

If there is no '}' character after lastPattern, `indexOf` returns -1, so the call becomes `uri.replace(startIndex, 0, value)`, which would replace from position 0, not the intended closing brace position. This could corrupt the URI string.
suspicion.suspected_bug: When a template parameter lacks a closing '}', uri.replace uses index 0 as end position instead of the actual closing brace, causing incorrect string replacement

bug:
`Reflector.getSetterType(String)` calls `setTypes.get(propertyName).getValue()` directly. When the property has no setter (for example a read-only property, or an unknown name), `setTypes.get(...)` returns `null`, so `.getValue()` throws a raw `NullPointerException` — before the `if (clazz == null)` check that is meant to raise the documented `ReflectionException`.

title: Throw a clear exception for an unclosed index bracket in PropertyTokenizer
bug:
`PropertyTokenizer` assumes that when a property name contains a `[`, its last character is the matching `]`:

```java
index = name.substring(delim + 1, name.length() - 1);
```

For a malformed expression with an unclosed bracket this misbehaves silently:
- `"foo[bar"` → `index` becomes `"ba"` (the last character is dropped),
- `"foo["` → `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

This validates the closing bracket and throws an `IllegalArgumentException` with a clear message for an unclosed bracket, instead of silently corrupting the index or throwing an opaque `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Valid expressions like `"foo[bar]"` are unaffected. Adds a regression test.

suspicion.observation: PropertyTokenizer constructor at line 39 finds '[' in name, and at line 41 extracts the index using `name.substring(delim + 1, name.length() - 1)`. This assumes there's always a closing ']' at the end of the string. If the property name is like "foo[bar" (no closing bracket), name.length() - 1 will point past the intended end, and substring will fail with StringIndexOutOfBoundsException because it looks for an index up to name.length()-1 but the '[' position + 1 might extend beyond what makes sense. Actually more precisely, if there's no closing bracket, substring(delim+1, name.length()-1) will just give everything from after '[' to the second-to-last char, which silently truncates the last character instead of properly reporting a parse error.
suspicion.suspected_bug: PropertyTokenizer silently truncates the last character when property name has an unclosed bracket like 'foo[bar' - it should throw an exception instead of producing incorrect parse results

title: Clear padding bits in BitMatrix.flip() so they are not read as set
bug:
`BitMatrix.flip()` (the no-arg variant) inverts every `int` in the `bits[]` array, including the unused padding bits beyond the logical width in each row's last `int` (`rowSize = (width + 31) / 32`, so a row whose width isn't a multiple of 32 has `rowSize * 32 - width` padding bits). After `flip()`, those stray bits are set, and methods that scan the raw bits — `getTopLeftOnBit()`, `getBottomRightOnBit()`, `getEnclosingRectangle()`, `equals()` — treat them as part of the matrix.

For example, on a `5×5` matrix, `flip()` then `getBottomRightOnBit()` returns `(31, 4)` instead of `(4, 4)`.

The fix masks off the padding bits in each row's last `int` after flipping. Adds a regression test.

Later methods like getTopLeftOnBit(), getBottomRightOnBit(), getEnclosingRectangle() and equals() will see these stray bits as if they were part of the matrix.
suspicion.suspected_bug: After calling flip(), padding bits beyond the logical matrix width become set to 1, causing getTopLeftOnBit()/getBottomRightOnBit()/getEnclosingRectangle() to return incorrect coordinates, and equals() to report false inequality with a clean matrix that was flipped back.
